question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The classic example that is normally quoted is Helter Skelter, the
White-Album closer.

The number is written in E major. The famous barn-storming intro is a
straight tonic statement, an E major / E5 power chord, and it is answered
immediately by the chord that lives a fifth up the scale. In E that fifth
degree is B and in the natural / Aeolian collection that the number uses
for its rock & roll riff the fifth degree is taken as minor, B minor.
In other words the opening gesture of the song is

    E  –  I
    Bm –  v

the tonic followed by the minor V, the “minor fifth” chord, often heard
in popular parlance as the tonic-to-fifth leap that opens the track and
that gives the piece its characteristic, almost tritone-like, jump.
It is the same I–v jump that is heard at the start of the Ticket to Ride /
I Feel Fine family of Beatles openers.  

In the strict tritone / tonic-to-bV reading the same gesture is the one
that is most often cited for I Want You (She’s So Heavy). The number is
in E and the first harmonic move that is heard after the opening E
tonic is the bV, B♭ major, i.e. an E → B♭ tritone jump, the textbook
tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-flat-five opening that the song is
known for.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The I - v leap that the Beatles use over and over in A is the one they open
*And I Love Her* / *We Can Work It Out* with. In the published key the verse is
essentially

A – Em – F♯m – D …

A major is the tonic of the verse and Em is the diatonic minor fifth, v. 
It is the same I-v opening that is normally quoted for *We Can Work It Out*,
A major tonic straight into its minor fifth Em, the A → E-minor jump that
opens the verse of *And I Love Her* and is the textbook Beatles I–v
opening. The minor-key analogue most often quoted is the i–v opening of
*Eleanor Rigby*, A minor → E minor.

3.text:
The opening that is usually quoted is the string intro to Eleanor Rigby.

The piece is in A minor.  The first two string chords that are heard are

* A minor – i, the tonic
* E minor – v, the minor triad built on the 5th degree of the A natural-
  minor scale

i → v is the classic tonic-to-minor-fifth jump, i.e. a tonic triad
immediately leaping up a perfect fifth to the diatonically minor fifth
chord. In the recording the A-minor ostinato is stated and then the
E-minor chord is entered on the very next bar, the i–v motion that
pervades the whole verse. The same i–v tonic-to-minor-fifth opening is
the one that is normally illustrated with the early rockers I Saw Her
Standing There / Help! – A major → E minor in major, the same
functional i/v motion – and it is the motion heard at the very start
of Eleanor Rigby.
